html:
The Spanish missions in California were a chain of 21 Catholic missions founded between 1769 and 1823 along the coast of what is now the US state of California. Franciscan friars ran them, guarded by Spanish soldiers, to convert the Native peoples and to hold Alta California for New Spain against Russian and British rivals.

The first, San Diego de Alcalá, was founded in 1769 under Junípero Serra. The chain ran north along the road called El Camino Real, ending at Sonoma in 1823.

The missions drew in nearby peoples such as the Kumeyaay, Chumash, Ohlone and Kizh. Once baptised, they were made to live in the mission, farm, herd and build, and were often not allowed to leave. Runaways were brought back by soldiers. Crowded quarters spread disease, and deaths far outran births. Many peoples lost most of their number within a generation, and some, such as the Luiseño, are still known by their mission's name.

After Mexico won independence, it secularised the missions from 1834 and their lands passed to private ranchos. Most Native survivors became ranch labourers. Worse came after 1848, with the Gold Rush and the California genocide. Many mission churches were later restored and are now landmarks.
